metadata.title: Basketball Blaster: Inside the Godot Code
metadata.audience: makers following the channel's Claude + Walker game workflows
metadata.note: godot-gamedev walker film. Code panels are Godot editor reconstructions with verbatim source; each is followed by real engine output of the same build. No game change, no paid calls, no upload.

beats.narration_text: Hola, this is Liam, in for Bear. That's the kind of prompt Walker expects, reconstructed here, not a transcript. This time we open the project itself: a piece of code, then the exact thing it does on screen, in the real build.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about Basketball Blaster: Fowl Play — Mr. Block, armed with a basketball gun and basketball grenades, collects every egg across three arenas while chickens pour out of pipes — into a playable Godot project.
props.runningText: illustrative reconstruction — not the historical prompt
output: Built: 8 thin scenes, 14 GDScript files and 1 shader, 2,408 lines.
Art reused from the Unity project; no automated tests.

beats.narration_text: Basketball Blaster is built in code. Its eight scene files are a few lines each, and twenty-four hundred lines of GDScript build everything else at runtime. So every piece of code we read has a result you can watch.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant writer: text is typed on screen over the narration, so mid-beat samples legitimately show a partial page. The finished text fills the safe area and holds for the last 1.5 s.

beats.narration_text: Open level one's scene file and there's one node. Run it, and game dot g d builds the rest: a World node holding the backdrop, decals, actors, projectiles and effects; every platform as a static body; three spotlights; the nests; a camera; and two canvas layers, one for the HUD and one for the fade. Most are never named, so the live tree reads at-Sprite2D-at-twenty-two.

props.title: Saved Scene vs. Live Tree
props.source: Live tree: printed from a running instance of res://scenes/level_1.tscn at 3 s, headless, no input, on an isolated copy (tree_probe.gd).

beats.narration_text: Here's the entire arena one scene: seven lines. One Node2D, game dot g d attached, and one exported number, level id, set to one. Arenas two and three are the same file with a different number. All the difference lives in a data table.

props.title: The Whole Arena Scene
props.code:
[gd_scene load_steps=2 format=3]

[ext_resource type="Script" path="res://scripts/game.gd" id="1_game"]

[node name="Level1" type="Node2D"]
script = ExtResource("1_game")
level_id = 1

beats.narration_text: That table is here. Arena three is one dictionary: forty-four tiles wide, a new chicken every two point two seconds per pipe, a cap of eighteen, four-hit chickens, four pipe columns, five spotlights, sixteen platforms as column, row and width, and seven eggs. Change a number, and the arena changes.
Arena three, built from that dictionary: four pipes, the navy tint, platforms up to row five, and chickens that take four hits.

beats.narration_text: Input is registered in code, not in the project settings. At boot, game state adds every action to Godot's InputMap: keys by physical position, both mouse buttons, and, a few lines further down, the joypad buttons and sticks. That's why one script can drive the keyboard, the mouse and a controller through the same actions.

props.title: Input Is Registered in Code
props.code:
func _configure_input() -> void:
	_add_keys("move_left", [KEY_A, KEY_LEFT])
	_add_keys("move_right", [KEY_D, KEY_RIGHT])
	_add_keys("move_down", [KEY_S, KEY_DOWN])
	_add_keys("jump", [KEY_SPACE, KEY_W, KEY_UP])
	_add_keys("fire", [KEY_F, KEY_J])
	_add_keys("grenade", [KEY_G, KEY_E])
	_add_keys("jetpack", [KEY_SHIFT])
	_add_keys("pause", [KEY_ESCAPE, KEY_P])
	_add_keys("restart", [KEY_R])

	_add_mouse("fire", MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT)
	_add_mouse("grenade", MOUSE_BUTTON_RIGHT)

notes.label: InputMap
notes.value: actions added at boot, not in project.godot

beats.narration_text: The jump handler. Down plus jump on a platform turns platform collisions off for a quarter second: that's the drop-through. Otherwise the press is buffered for twelve hundredths of a second. On the floor, or within coyote time, it jumps. In the air, it spends the one double jump.

props.title: Jump, Buffer, Coyote, Double

beats.narration_text: First press: a jump. Second press, in mid-air: the double jump, and he climbs again before gravity wins.

beats.narration_text: The jetpack, which Unity declared and never used. While Shift is held and fuel remains, it burns fuel at one second per second and pushes velocity upward, capped at four hundred and thirty pixels a second. It also resets time in air, so the extra fall gravity waits.

props.title: The Jetpack Unity Never Wired Up

beats.narration_text: Shift held: the flame, the climb, and the blue fuel bar running down.

beats.narration_text: Weapons sit in one function. Holding fire spawns a ball whenever the cooldown hits zero, every four tenths of a second. The grenade needs a fresh press and has its own cooldown. Neither spawns anything itself: the player emits a signal, and the arena builds the projectile.

props.title: Weapons Emit, the Arena Builds

beats.narration_text: Held left click: a steady stream of basketballs toward the crosshair, each with a muzzle flash and a small recoil.

beats.narration_text: The grenade is a rigid body with a fuse. Every physics frame it adds time to a countdown. Three blinks are spaced across three seconds, each a red light and a beep signal, and at three seconds it explodes. Touching a chicken explodes it early.

props.title: A Rigid Body With a Fuse

beats.narration_text: Right-click: the grenade arcs out, bounces, blinks, and blows, and the screen shakes.

beats.narration_text: One ten-line shader does two jobs. A tint uniform multiplies the sprite's colour, which is how a pipe paints its chicken one of eight palette colours. A flash uniform mixes toward white: the hit flash. The script sets flash to one, and a tween resets it a tenth of a second later.

props.title: One Shader, Two Jobs

notes.label: flash
notes.value: white for 0.1 s on a hit

beats.narration_text: Chickens in different tints from the same white sprite sheet, and every ball that lands flashes its target white for a tenth of a second.

beats.narration_text: Each chicken death adds a kill and bumps a counter. The first death in a frame defers a check to the next physics frame. If three or more died by then, it's a mega kill: sound, floating text and shake. It's the same window Unity's audio manager used.

props.title: Three Deaths, One Frame
props.code:
func _on_chicken_died(chicken: CharacterBody2D) -> void:
	var at := chicken.global_position
	Fx.feathers(effects, at, chicken.tint)
	Fx.splatter(decals, at + Vector2(0, 10))
	kills += 1
	deaths_this_window += 1
	if not death_window_open:
		death_window_open = true
		_resolve_death_window.call_deferred(at)

func _resolve_death_window(at: Vector2) -> void:
	# Unity AudioManager.DeathWindowRoutine: three or more deaths in one frame earn a megakill.
	await get_tree().physics_frame
	if deaths_this_window >= MEGA_KILL_AMOUNT:
		Audio.play("megakill")
		Fx.floating_text(effects, at + Vector2(0, -50), "MEGA KILL!", GameState.LIME, 46)
		_shake(10.0)
	Audio.play("splat")
	deaths_this_window = 0
	death_window_open = false

beats.narration_text: One grenade, four deaths before the next physics frame: mega kill. And again, at a quarter of the speed, labelled as a replay.

beats.narration_text: Contact damage is a distance check, not a physics collision. Every frame, unless the player is invulnerable, the arena measures the distance to each live chicken. Under fifty-eight pixels, it's a hit: one health, a sound, a shake, a knockback. At zero health, a life is lost.

props.title: Contact Is a Distance Check

beats.narration_text: Walking into the flock: a hit and a knockback, another, and the third costs the life, followed by the fade and the respawn at the gate.

beats.narration_text: Eggs use the same idea. Each frame, every nest closer than sixty-two pixels is collected: a sparkle, plus-one-egg text, the counter. The loop walks backwards, so removing a nest mid-loop is safe. When the count reaches the arena's total, the level completes.

props.title: Eggs Use the Same Idea

beats.narration_text: Egg after egg on the route, the counter ticking, and the last one ends the arena: court cleared.

beats.narration_text: Now a defect, in the code. The briefing advances on ui accept, or on any mouse button press, but only in unhandled input. A few lines below, build screen adds a full-screen shade ColorRect. A ColorRect stops mouse events by default, so the click is consumed as GUI input and never arrives.

props.title: Where the Click Goes

notes.label: Advances on
notes.value: ui_accept or any mouse press, in _unhandled_input

notes.label: Shade
notes.value: ColorRect, mouse filter STOP by default

beats.narration_text: And the consequence: two clicks, on and above the dialogue box, and nothing happens. Enter advances at once.

beats.narration_text: And a second layout defect, in the HUD's bar helper. It sets the bar's size before it turns show percentage off. A probe of the running game measures both bars at thirty-four pixels tall, not fourteen. The likely cause is that order: the size is clamped to the taller minimum the percentage text still needed.

props.title: A Bar That Grew
props.code:
func _make_bar(at: Vector2, bar_size: Vector2, fill: Color) -> ProgressBar:
	var bar := ProgressBar.new()
	bar.position = at
	bar.size = bar_size
	bar.show_percentage = false
	bar.add_theme_stylebox_override("background", GameState.panel_style(Color(0.02, 0.08, 0.14, 0.9), GameState.INK, 5, 1))
	bar.add_theme_stylebox_override("fill", GameState.panel_style(fill, Color.TRANSPARENT, 5, 0))
	return bar

beats.narration_text: Zoomed into the real frame: the bars run over their own hint labels, RMB slash G, and SHIFT, while the fuel bar drains.

beats.narration_text: The rest of the project, in one pass. A main menu, How to Play, and one end-screen script that serves both victory and defeat through an exported mode. An Audio autoload that loads thirteen named sounds into sixteen pooled voices. A static effects library for feathers, splatter, dust and the explosion. Fifty-six images and three fonts, mostly reused from the Unity project. Six of those images, and one font, are never used. And there is no test folder at all.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. This is a project you can read top to bottom: thin scenes, data tables, signals between player and arena, and one shader doing two jobs. The two defects I found are input plumbing and layout: places where the logic is right and the screen isn't. There are no tests, and a person still has to play it.

artifactLines: Implemented: 8 thin scenes, 2,408 lines of GDScript, arenas as data tables.
Good habits: player and arena talk by signals; one shader for tint and flash.
Defects on screen: a shade eats briefing clicks; HUD bars draw over their labels.
Missing: automated tests. Not judged: fun, balance — 0 human playtests.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude in your own Godot project: Use Walker on my Godot project. Pick one UI control and predict what a mouse click does: which node receives the event, and which nodes could swallow it first. Then write a capture that proves or disproves it with real input, and only after that, propose the smallest code change. Make the prediction before you look. Liam, in for Bear.
